<meta>continues from previous page: they are not laboring</meta> in vain in the rest of their endeavors. They even advertise themselves to others to gain a better reputation for the things in which they are occupied. Thus it happens that, in the manner of <term>Atalanta</term> <gloss>a mythological huntress who lost a race because she stopped to pick up golden apples</gloss>, they go off the path to pick up the golden apple. Meanwhile, they interrupt their course and let victory slip from their hands. But in the true racecourse of Experience, and in producing new works from it, Divine Wisdom and Order must be taken entirely as the model. For God on the first day of Creation created only Light, and assigned a whole day to that work; he did not create any material work on that day. Similarly, from all kinds of Experience, the discovery of true <term>Causes</term> and <term>Axioms</term> <gloss>established principles or laws</gloss> must first be drawn out. One should seek <term>lucifera</term> <gloss>light-bearing</gloss> experiments, not <term>fructifera</term> <gloss>fruit-bearing</gloss> ones <note>Bacon distinguishes between experiments that provide knowledge, which he calls light-bearing, and those that provide immediate practical utility, which he calls fruit-bearing</note>. Axioms that are rightly discovered and established do not provide for <term>Praxis</term> <gloss>practice or application</gloss> in a restricted way, but in abundance; they draw after them ranks and troops of Works. But we shall speak later about the ways of experimenting, which are no less blocked and closed off than the ways of Judging. For the present, we have spoken only of common Experience as a poor form of <term>Demonstration</term> <gloss>the process of proving a conclusion</gloss>. Now the order of things requires that we add something about those signs we mentioned a little while ago, namely, that the Philosophies and Contemplations in use are in a bad state. We must also speak about the Causes of a situation that seems so wonderful and incredible at first sight. For the knowledge of the signs prepares the way for agreement; but the explanation of the causes removes the sense of a miracle. These two things help much toward a gentler and easier uprooting of the <term>Idols</term> <gloss>prejudices or false notions</gloss> from the Understanding.

<summary>Bacon argues that researchers often prioritize immediate practical results over the discovery of fundamental principles, comparing them to Atalanta being distracted by golden apples. He asserts that the search for light-bearing experiments must precede the search for fruit-bearing ones to truly advance science.</summary>
<keywords>Atalanta, light-bearing experiments, fruit-bearing experiments, Axioms, Practice, Idols of the Mind, scientific method, Divine Wisdom</keywords>
